teaches: DCC core noun; Rome is simply Urbs
context: Romans called Rome just 'the City'. Popes still bless 'urbī et orbī' — to the City and the world. English 'urban', 'suburb' come from it.

image_idea.description: Model of ancient Rome (Museo della Civiltà Romana), wide crop

context: The Via Appia, begun 312 BC by Appius Claudius, ran from Rome to Capua and later Brundisium. Its paving stones are still walkable today.

image_idea.description: Via Appia paving with tombs, portrait crop

latin: Rōma urbs est. Via longa est.
translation: Rome is a city. The road is long.
context: Latin usually puts the verb last, but 'est' can float. Start every sentence by finding the verb, then its subject in the nominative.
Most -a nouns are feminine. Legend says a lupa nursed Romulus and Remus; 'lupa' was also slang for a prostitute, which ancient writers used to rationalise the myth.

translation: The Senate and the Roman People
context: The formula named the Roman state on coins, arches and standards. Rome's manhole covers still carry it. Note -que glued to the second word: populus-que.

image_idea.description: Modern Rome manhole cover with SPQR or Arch of Titus attic

translation: The seven hills: Palatine, Capitoline, Aventine…
teaches: Place names in the nominative; map-tap game
context: Tap each hill as you hear its Latin name. The Palatine gave English 'palace', because emperors built their homes there.

image_idea.description: Public-domain map of the seven hills of Rome

latin: pater, patris m.; māter, mātris f.
context: The paterfamilias held legal power (patria potestās) over his household, even adult sons. Mothers like Cornelia shaped sons' education and reputation.

image_idea.description: Roman funerary relief of a married couple (Met)
image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

context: Roman names showed descent: 'M. F.' on inscriptions means Mārcī fīlius, son of Marcus. Compare Agrippa's L·F on the Pantheon.

image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

latin: Pater fīlium amat. Fīlium pater amat.
translation: The father loves the son. (same meaning)
teaches: Accusative marks the object, so word order is free
context: Endings, not position, show who does what: -um/-am object, -us/-a subject. Swap word order and the meaning stays.

image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

context: Enslaved people (servī) were part of the familia. Neuter nouns like dōnum look the same as subject and object.

image_idea.description: Mosaic of servants serving a banquet (Bardo/Commons)

latin: familia, domus → family, domestic, domicile, paternal, maternal
context: A Roman familia meant the whole household, slaves included. Domus gives 'domestic' and 'dome'; pater gives 'paternal', 'patron', 'patriot'.

image_idea.description: House of the Vettii atrium, Pompeii

teaches: Daily life vocab; 1st decl. noun + adjective agreement
context: Freeborn Roman boys wore a bulla amulet until about age 16, when they dedicated it to the household gods (Larēs) and put on the adult toga.

image_idea.description: Etruscan/Roman gold bulla, cut-out (Met or Walters)
image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

latin: Haec ornāmenta sunt mea. — Cornēlia? Līvia? Lucrētia?
translation: These are my jewels — who said it?
teaches: Recall of quote card; demonstratives haec
context: Pick the speaker. Answer: Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, per Valerius Maximus 4.4 pr. Links to existing card in rome-cards.json.

image_idea.description: Cornelia painting (Angelica Kauffman) cut to arch

source.work: Valerius Maximus, Facta et dicta memorabilia

teaches: Core noun; preview of 3rd-decl. stem change
context: A legionary served about 25 years under Augustus' reforms. English 'military', 'militia' keep the stem mīlit-.

image_idea.description: Cut-out legionary statue or tombstone relief

context: Every night on campaign a legion dug a fortified camp. Place names ending -chester, -caster, -cester (Lancaster, Chester) descend from castra.

translation: The soldiers march. The legion fights.
context: Chant the endings like a marching cadence. Plural -nt vs singular -t tells you how many are acting.

translation: The centurion sees and warns the soldiers.
context: Centurions led roughly 80 men and carried a vine-stick (vītis) as a badge of rank. Their tombstones often show it.

image_idea.description: Tombstone of centurion M. Caelius (Bonn), portrait

latin: … spērābō tē, soror. Valē, soror, anima mea …
translation: … I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul …
teaches: Real handwriting from a fort; letter farewell formulae (valē, vocative)
context: Claudia Severa invited Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday about AD 100: the earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman, found at Vindolanda.
Legionaries threw the pilum before closing in. Its soft iron shank bent on impact so enemies could not throw it back, according to Caesar-era practice and archaeology.

image_idea.description: Reconstructed pilum or Roman sword, cut-out

context: Tap each chunk to expand it. Legion XX served in Britain; its boar emblem appears on stamped tiles and building stones from Chester and Hadrian's Wall.
Literally 'the public thing'. English 'republic' comes straight from it; Cicero wrote a dialogue titled Dē rē pūblicā.
'Senātus' comes from senex, old man: a council of elders. Two consuls were elected yearly, and years were named after them.

translation: the Forum of the Romans; the Temple of Saturn
context: Saturn's temple held the state treasury (aerārium). Its eight columns still stand at the Forum's west end.

image_idea.description: Temple of Saturn columns, portrait crop

translation: The Senate gives honours to Caesar.
context: In 44 BC the Senate heaped honours on Caesar, including dictator for life. Weeks later senators killed him in the Curia of Pompey.

latin: vir bonus, fēmina bona, templum bonum
translation: good man, good woman, good temple
context: Adjectives copy their noun's gender, number and case. Cato defined the orator as vir bonus dīcendī perītus — a good man skilled in speaking (via Quintilian 12.1.1).

image_idea.description: Cut-out bust of Cato-type Roman elder
image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

context: Only citizens could wear the toga. Candidates for office whitened theirs with chalk (toga candida), giving English 'candidate'.

latin: dīcō, dīcere, dīxī, dictum → dictate, diction, verdict, predict
context: Root dict- runs through law and rhetoric: a dictator was one whose word was law. Cicero's speeches made dīcere the orator's verb.
Romans honoured many gods; deī and dī are both plural forms. English 'deity', 'divine' (from dīvus) come from this family.

image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

context: Originally templum meant a space marked out by augurs for watching birds. English 'contemplate' kept that idea of watching.

latin: rēx, rēgis; lēx, lēgis; pāx, pācis
teaches: 3rd declension: learn the genitive to find the stem
context: The nominative hides the stem; the genitive reveals it. Rome expelled its kings (rēgēs) traditionally in 509 BC and hated the word rēx afterward.

latin: in templō, cum deīs, ex urbe
translation: in the temple, with the gods, out of the city
teaches: Prepositions + ablative (in, cum, ex/ē, ā/ab, dē, sine)
context: Mnemonic: SID & CAPPE. The fire of Vesta burned in aede Vestae, guarded by six Vestal Virgins.

translation: Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made this
teaches: Parse-the-inscription game built on existing card i-pantheon-agrippa
context: Drag each abbreviation to its full form. Reuses CIL VI 896 already verified-pending in rome-cards; here it tests abbreviations and the perfect fēcit as a preview.
Every house had a lararium where the family offered food and wine to the Lares. Painted lararia survive at Pompeii, often with a snake guardian.

image_idea.description: Lararium, House of the Vettii, Pompeii

context: Imperātor was a title soldiers shouted for a victorious general. Augustus turned it into a permanent name, giving us 'emperor'.

latin: Bella terrā et marī cīvīlia externaque tōtō in orbe terrārum saepe gessī.
translation: I often waged wars, civil and foreign, on land and sea throughout the whole world.
context: Augustus' own account of his deeds was inscribed on bronze pillars at his mausoleum. The best copy survives in Ankara.

image_idea.description: Res Gestae wall at Ankara (Monumentum Ancyranum)

latin: Urbem … marmoream sē relinquere, quam latericiam accēpisset (Suet.) / Rōmānī lateribus aedificābant.
translation: (He boasted) that he left as marble the city he had received as brick. / The Romans used to build with bricks.
context: Suetonius reports Augustus' boast; the imperfect describes ongoing past habit, the perfect completed acts.

translation: I can, you can, s/he can
context: Learn sum first, then glue pot- on (pos- before s). Pairs with an infinitive: venīre possum, I can come.

image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

context: Octavian stressed his adoption by the deified Julius on coins. DIVI F = dīvī fīlius, a powerful propaganda line before the name Augustus (27 BC).

image_idea.description: Denarius of Octavian, CAESAR DIVI F (ANS/Met)
image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

context: A denarius was worth four sesterces. 'Dēnārius' (from dēnī, ten each) gave the 'd' in old British £sd and the word 'dinar'.

image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

latin: Augustus, Tiberius, Claudius, Nerō, Trāiānus, Hadriānus
teaches: Ordering game with nominative names and dates
context: Drag emperors onto the timeline. Trajan's conquests brought the empire to its largest extent in AD 117.

image_idea.description: Cut-out busts from Met/Commons, one per emperor
image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

teaches: Model 1st conjugation verb with principal parts
context: Catullus' poems to 'Lesbia' made amō the poet's verb. Its parts are the pattern for all regular 1st-conjugation verbs.

image_idea.description: Fresco of a couple, Pompeii (Terentius Neo)

latin: Carpe diem, quam minimum crēdula posterō.
translation: Pluck the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow.
context: Horace ends an ode to Leuconoe with this line: harvest today like ripe fruit. Imperatives: stem alone (amā, vidē, carpe), plural -te.

image_idea.description: Horace manuscript or Horace portrait medallion

context: Horace closes Odes 3 confident his poetry will outlive him. Links to the existing 'Exēgī monumentum' card.

latin: Ego, tū; mē, tē; mihi, tibi
translation: I, you; me, you; to me, to you
context: Poetry is full of ego and tū. Ovid's lover tells his girl to come to him: personal pronouns carry the drama of address.

image_idea.description: Ovid portrait or statue at Constanța

context: Virgil's 'fugit irreparābile tempus' and Ovid's 'tempus edāx rērum' both use it. English 'temporary', 'contemporary', 'tempo'.

image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

translation: I sing of arms and the man…
teaches: Hear dactylic hexameter: long/short tap rhythm
context: Tap along to a human reading of Aeneid 1.1 in restored pronunciation. Learners feel vowel length, which reinforces macrons.
Stoics trained the animus to stay calm. English 'animate', 'animal', 'unanimous' (ūnus + animus).

translation: To live, my Lucilius, is to be a soldier.
context: Seneca compares life to military service in his letters to Lucilius. Infinitives end -re and can act as nouns.

translation: They say that Romulus founded the city.
context: Latin has no word for 'that' here: the subject goes accusative, the verb infinitive. Livy uses this constantly to report legends he doubts.

image_idea.description: Romulus and Remus on Lupa, cut-out

latin: videō, vidēre, vīdī, vīsum → video, vision, evident, provide, visa
context: Philosophers prized seeing truly. Your 'video' is literally 'I see'; 'provide' is to see ahead.

image_idea.description: Roman fresco eye/portrait of a woman (Sappho fresco)

latin: Marcus Aurēlius Latīnē scrīpsit 'Ad sē ipsum'. Vērum an falsum?
translation: Marcus Aurelius wrote 'To Himself' in Latin. True or false?
teaches: Comprehension in simple Latin; cultural accuracy
context: False: the Meditations are in Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans. Bilingualism was normal among the elite.

image_idea.description: Equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius, Capitoline, cut-out

context: Roman children learned letters with a grammaticus or lūdī magister, writing on wax tablets with a stylus — whose flat end erased mistakes.
Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in 410. The shock prompted Augustine to write the City of God. Present passive: -tur (capitur, 'is captured').

latin: ☧ (Chī-Rhō) on coins of Constantine; Vulgate: Ego sum α et ω
translation: Chi-Rho; I am Alpha and Omega
teaches: Reading Christian symbols on late Roman coins
context: Constantine adopted the Chi-Rho after 312. Later coins pair it with Alpha and Omega from Revelation (Apoc. 1:8 in the Vulgate).

image_idea.description: Late Roman coin or silver plate with Chi-Rho
image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

teaches: Core vocab revisited in a new era
context: After 476 Germanic kings ruled the West in Latin. Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus; Theodoric ruled Italy as rēx.

latin: Ego sum via, et vēritās, et vīta.
translation: I am the way, and the truth, and the life.
context: Jerome's Vulgate (c. 382–405) became the West's Bible for a millennium. Its plain Latin is ideal reading for beginners.

latin: crux, crucis → crucial, crucify, crusade, excruciating
context: Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, abolished by Constantine. 'Excruciating' literally means 'out of the cross'; 'crucial' first meant a crossroads.

image_idea.description: Early Christian cross or ivory panel (Met)
image_idea.license_status: CC0 (Met Open Access); verify object page

context: Rome fed citizens free grain, later bread. Losing Egypt and Africa's grain helped starve the late western capital; Juvenal's 'pānem et circēnsēs' card connects here.

latin: Pater noster, quī es in caelīs
translation: Our Father, who art in heaven
context: The Lord's Prayer (Matt. 6:9) was the first Latin many medieval people learned. Already in medieval-cards; here it drives a relative-clause drill.

latin: liber, librī m.; legō, legere, lēgī, lēctum
context: Monks copied books in the scriptorium. 'Library', 'lecture', 'legend' (things to be read). Don't confuse liber (book) with līber (free).

teaches: Monastic vocab; Greek loans in Latin
context: Benedict's Rule organised the day into hours of prayer and work. 'Monk' and 'abbot' come from Greek and Aramaic through Latin.

teaches: Medieval coin legend reusing Roman titles
context: Charlemagne, crowned in 800, issued coins styling himself like a Roman emperor. Compare with Augustus' coins in Unit 6.

translation: Here ends the book… Pray for the scribe.
teaches: Parse a scribe's colophon; imperative plural review
context: Scribes often signed off with a request for prayer or a complaint about cold fingers. 'Explicit' (it is unrolled) ended books; 'incipit' began them.

latin: Lindisfarna, Iona, Sanctus Gallus, Aquīsgrānum, Rōma
translation: Lindisfarne, Iona, St Gall, Aachen, Rome
context: Tap where Latin learning survived and spread: Irish and Northumbrian monasteries, St Gall, Charlemagne's court at Aachen.

latin: scrībō, scrībere, scrīpsī, scrīptum → scribe, script, describe, manuscript
teaches: Derivatives; manū scrīptum = written by hand
context: A 'manuscript' is literally manū scrīptus, written by hand. Ties to the Scriba rank in the reward ladder.
